title: Inside ARTEX: AI Hacking Tools, Exposed Servers and South Korean Bank Breaches
excerpt: Inside ARTEX: AI Hacking Tools, Exposed Servers and South Korean Bank Breaches. Inside ARTEX: AI Hacking Tools, Exposed Servers and South Korean Bank Breaches. Pierluigi Paganini November 07, 2026. Hunt. io traced ARTEX servers and AI-powered hacking tools used in breaches affecting seven South Korean financial institutions. Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions had data breached through internet-facing systems. About 66,000 to 67,000 people and around 2,200 corporations were affected, and personal, employment, income and loan data was exposed. Hunt. io dug into the infrastructure behind the campaign , and its findings add a lot to what CrowdStrike and Genians already published. CrowdStrike reported on October 7 and Genians Security Center on October 12 , and both pointed to ARTEX , an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework developed in China and licensed under AGPL-3. 0. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by money ran it, and not an established threat group. DeepSeek v4. 1 Flash was the main model, with GLM 5. 3 and Grok 4. 6 as backups, reached partly through a reseller domain, xcai[. ]pro. The public indicators were a server at 38. 244. 50[. ]120, which hosted the ARTEX console, plus a Hong Kong address and nine proxies. Genians said the ARTEX GitHub repository and Docker image were removed on October 11, though forks and mirrors remain. “CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the operator was a single Chinese-speaking individual motivated by financial gain rather than an established threat group. ” reads the report published by Hunt. io. “The infrastructure reportedly accessed these services in part through the reseller domain xcai[. ]pro. Both reports described a two-server configuration, consisting of a Hong Kong-based IP address used as primary infrastructure and 38. 244. 50[. ]120 , which hosted the ARTEX console. ”. Hunt. io notified the relevant national CERT before publishing, and says the report holds no personal records or credentials. The company’s own scanning showed 38. 244. 50[. ]120 sits on Cogent’s network in Los Angeles, with 15 open ports. The ARTEX login page, with a Chinese title meaning “autonomous penetration testing console”, appears on ports 443 and 8090. Other services include a Gemini2API admin console and a Tinyproxy server. Searching its AttackCapture platform for that address, Hunt. io found another open directory at 23. 248. 226[. ]250, a jump server in Hong Kong on AS138415. It held 42 files in 2 subdirectories, 105 MB in all, and the platform had logged warnings on September 5, September 26 and October 5. A file in it names 38. 244. 50[. ]120 as the jump host, and its own comment tells the operator never to paste the credentials into a session. It sat in an open directory. Three scripts back up the link. They keep reverse SSH tunnels alive, run a local relay, and copy files to the jump host, one tunnel is named grok2api, and the credentials file also holds keys for Zhipu AI’s GLM models, an OpenAI-compatible relay and a proxy service. That explains how several language models ran in one campaign. The AI setup is the most striking part. A state file shows the harness is Claude Code itself, version 2. 1. 221, started 510 times since August 4, but it isn’t talking to Anthropic. A small proxy, ds-models-shim. py, fixes a compatibility problem by faking a model list and sending requests to DeepSeek, and another, xcai-effort-shim. py, adds a reasoning setting because the DeepSeek backend otherwise skips its reasoning step. The route runs from Claude Code through Claude Code Router, an open-source project, to xcai and then to DeepSeek. “A small local proxy, ds-models-shim. py , addresses a compatibility issue: the official /v1/models endpoint returns a 404 response when queried against a non-Anthropic backend, preventing Claude Code from discovering the availabl

OCC Issues Supervisory Framework for Banks’ Use of “Super Intelligence”: A Risk-Based Approach to Generative and Agentic AI
excerpt: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has taken another important step in addressing the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence in the banking industry. On November 4, 2026, the OCC issued a new supervisory framework designed to assist its bank examiners in evaluating banks’ use of what the agency, following the terminology adopted by the Trump Administration, calls “Super Intelligence” (SI). The framework focuses particularly on generative AI and agentic AI and provides examiners with a detailed roadmap for evaluating the risks associated with these technologies and the controls banks have implemented to manage those risks. Importantly, the OCC emphasizes that the framework is intended as a resource for examiners, not as a source of new regulatory requirements for banks. It does not establish a separate category of supervisory risk for SI, require banks to adopt a separate SI risk appetite, or impose new enforceable standards. Rather, it directs examiners to consider how the use of SI may introduce, amplify, or modify risks that banks already manage under established supervisory frameworks. That distinction is significant, particularly at a time when financial institutions are seeking greater regulatory clarity concerning the use of generative and agentic AI. The OCC’s approach: Technology-neutral supervision rather than a new regulatory regime. The new framework implements the OCC’s commitment to encourage responsible technological innovation while maintaining the safety and soundness of the banking system and compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The OCC recognizes that SI can provide substantial benefits to banks and their customers, including more efficient customer service, improved fraud detection, stronger cybersecurity, reduced operational costs, and greater automation of manual processes. At the same time, the agency acknowledges that the rapid evolution of generative and agentic AI presents risks that may not be adequately addressed by controls developed for traditional technologies. The OCC makes clear, however, that examiners should not treat SI as a separate and distinct risk category. Nor should banks be required to establish a separate SI risk appetite. Instead, SI-related risks should be incorporated into existing risk-management frameworks, including those addressing operational risk, compliance risk, credit risk, model risk, cybersecurity, privacy, and third-party relationships. This approach is consistent with the OCC’s broader emphasis on technology-neutral supervision. The agency intends to evaluate the risks presented by a particular application rather than impose restrictions merely because a bank employs a new or sophisticated technology. The OCC also emphasizes proportionality. Examiners should exercise judgment based on the bank’s size, complexity, risk profile, and the nature and potential consequences of its particular SI applications. Six pillars and sixteen components. The framework identifies six principal pillars around which examiners should organize their evaluation of a bank’s use of SI:. Purpose – Establishing the actions that an SI system or agent is authorized to perform. Risk – Assessing the consequences if the system’s output or actions are inaccurate, inappropriate, or otherwise unsuitable. Control – Establishing safeguards against unauthorized, inappropriate, or unsafe actions. Oversight – Identifying who monitors the system and who is accountable for its use. Resilience – Ensuring that the bank can detect, contain, recover from, and remediate system failures while maintaining critical operations. Assurance – Establishing that controls continue to operate effectively through testing, documentation, independent review, and third-party oversight. title: Moment Appoints SIMON Founder Jason Broder As Strategic Advisor To Expand AI-Powered Wealth Management Platform
excerpt: . Moment Appoints SIMON Founder Jason Broder As Strategic Advisor To Expand AI-Powered Wealth Management Platform. Moment, a New York-based artificial intelligence technology company serving investment management firms, has appointed Jason Broder as a strategic advisor. Broder, the founder and former CEO of SIMON and a former iCapital executive, brings extensive experience building financial technology platforms for wealth management institutions and financial advisors. The appointment supports Moment’s efforts to expand its AI-powered investment management platform, which uses AI agents to assist financial advisors and operational teams. Broder founded SIMON in 2012 while at Goldman Sachs, where the platform was originally developed to help financial advisors access structured investment products. In 2018, he led SIMON’s separation from Goldman Sachs, supported by a consortium of banking institutions. The business later expanded across the wealth management industry, with its platform used by more than 100,000 financial professionals nationwide by 2021. Broder served as SIMON’s CEO until iCapital acquired the company in 2022. After the transaction, he became Chief Product Officer at iCapital, helping develop technology that supports alternative investment access and investment management workflows. Before founding SIMON, Broder spent 17 years at Goldman Sachs, ultimately serving as a Managing Director and Head of the Private Investor Product Group. His career provides experience spanning financial product development, investment distribution, technology commercialization, and enterprise financial services. At Moment, Broder will advise the leadership team as the company expands its adoption among investment management organizations. Moment develops a unified technology platform that incorporates AI agents into investment management operations, with the goal of supporting financial advisors and the teams responsible for servicing investment accounts. The company’s technology is designed to help organizations improve operational efficiency and incorporate artificial intelligence into existing workflows. Moment works with financial institutions that collectively oversee more than $10 trillion in assets and support more than 60,000 financial advisors. Its customers include organizations seeking to modernize investment management processes while maintaining the infrastructure required to serve institutional and individual investors. The company is backed by venture capital investors Andreessen Horowitz and Index Ventures. Broder’s experience building SIMON into a widely adopted wealth management technology platform is expected to provide strategic guidance as Moment develops additional AI capabilities and expands its relationships with financial institutions. KEY QUOTES. “Moment is at the frontier in wealth management. They combine next-generation infrastructure with AI that drives real growth and ROI for their clients. I’ve never seen a firm who delivers this quickly with such flawless execution — their clients love it. ”. Jason Broder, Strategic Advisor To Moment And Founder Of SIMON. “Jason is one of the few people in wealth management that understands what it takes to change the industry. I’ve admired his work for years, and we couldn’t be more excited to have him with us. ”. Dylan Parker, Co-Founder And CEO Of Moment.

rules.useCaseEvidence: The appointment supports Moment’s efforts to expand its AI-powered investment management platform, which uses AI agents to assist financial advisors and operational teams.

title: AI protocols fuel ‘code red’ at big banks, fintech CEO says
summary: As banks such as PNC and Fifth Third draw boundaries for what they’ll let agents do, the fintech Socure is debuting an AI agent detection tool to help.
excerpt: An article from. AI protocols fuel ‘code red’ at big banks, fintech CEO says. As banks such as PNC and Fifth Third draw boundaries for what they’ll let agents do, the fintech Socure is debuting an AI agent detection tool to help. Published Nov. 6, 2026. Caitlin Mullen Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. The CEO of a fintech that works with big banks expects it’ll be about six months before lenders establish clear protocols around what agents can and can’t do on behalf of customers. As AI agent use takes off and banks consider access questions, “there’s a lot of code reds going on in the banks right now,” Socure CEO Johnny Ayers said in a recent interview. Socure, an identity and risk intelligence provider, works with about 3,000 banks, including 19 of the top 20 in the U. S. , and about 700 fintechs, Ayers said. “I think we're still a ways out from the banks having a clear protocol around when [a person can] go open a new bank account or a credit card with her agent,” Ayers said. AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, Instinct and OpenAI’s dots, acting on behalf of consumers, have quickly proliferated in recent weeks, prompting banks to throw up walls and bank CEOs to warn of potential liability issues. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citi have all blocked AI agent access to customer accounts. Yet Axios has reported top U. S. banks have discovered AI agents within accounts anyway, with some agents taking actions that went beyond their instructions. Banks are “built on standards and protocols, and, I think, are probably taking a defensive stance while they get the rules and protocols with the networks in place,” Ayers said. There’s plenty for banks and other industry players to sort through and establish parameters around, as well as how regulators might respond if there are customer issues, Ayers said. Meanwhile, the technology is evolving rapidly. “You're seeing the vulnerabilities in cyber. People are kind of scared,” Ayers said. “Folks are definitely taking more of a wait-and-see [approach]. ”. “You have thousands of people in these banks that are working to basically patch all of the critical vulnerabilities that [Anthropic’s Claude] Mythos and others are highlighting. And so that's not an organization they generally want agents running rampant in,” he added. The fraud, anti-money laundering and know-your-customer framework is not yet written for agents, he noted. “Can an agent open a bank account on your behalf? What is it allowed to do? What are its limits?”. “There’s an acceleration right now” on the bank and card issuer side, “to try to figure out what agents are allowed to do,” Ayers said. There are also data access concerns. “You have this rightful blocking to make sure that these agents aren't going in and basically siphoning off transaction data on behalf of consumers, where consumers are unknowingly giving access,” Ayers said. Banks have more control over mobile use, Ayers said, but with web applications, “they need to figure this out now, because I can let an agent take over my browser entirely. ”. He pointed to a juxtaposition between fintech and bank approaches. The latter are “at such big scale, they have the luxury of waiting and seeing,” Ayers said, where fintechs such as Mercury are taking the opposite approach. Bank reactions. PNC CEO Bill Demchak, at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas last month, said agent-only transactions will never happen. During a Friday appearance at the BancAnalysts Association of Boston conference , Demchak added “the notion of agentic execution versus agentic suggestion, I think, is a very different thing. ”. “We won’t let an agent come in and click buttons – in effect, move money on your behalf – without you in the loop, authentication on us, agreeing to the transaction,” which is “tablestakes,” the CEO of the Pittsburgh-based bank said. title: Rex Africa Launches Nigeria’s First AI-Native Bank With Personalised Financial Services - Brand Spur
excerpt: Banking and Finance. Brand News. Tech. WhatsApp. Facebook. Twitter. Linkedin. Telegram. Email. Print. Shares. Share. Post. Pin. Email. Share. Rex Africa has launched what it describes as Nigeria’s first artificial intelligence ( AI )-native bank, introducing a digital banking platform that combines everyday financial services with personalised financial guidance for individuals and businesses. The bank, powered by Rex Microfinance Bank Limited, is built around Rex Atlas, an AI-powered financial agent designed to help customers understand their spending, manage savings, access credit and make more informed financial decisions. According to Brandspur Banking News Desk, the launch comes as Nigeria continues to expand financial inclusion, with increasing attention on whether access to banking services is translating into better financial outcomes for consumers. Figures from the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) indicate that financial inclusion rose from 64 per cent in 2023 to 73 per cent in 2026. However, the survey findings cited by Rex Africa suggest that only about one in four Nigerian adults is financially healthy, highlighting the gap between having a bank account and effectively managing personal finances. Rex says its platform is designed to address that gap by integrating artificial intelligence into its banking infrastructure from the outset, rather than introducing it as an additional feature. Its proprietary technology, RexCore, provides the underlying banking infrastructure, while Rex Atlas serves as the intelligence layer through which customers can interact with the platform and receive personalised financial guidance. Through the AI-powered agent, users can seek guidance on saving, investing, accessing credit and managing financial risks. The system is also designed to analyse customers’ financial histories and offer recommendations based on their individual circumstances and goals. The platform includes several financial products for individuals and businesses. RexSave provides flexible savings, while RexVault offers fixed-term savings with returns. RexFlex provides access to credit, and RexCard supports everyday payments. See Also: Flutterwave Secures Nigerian Banking Licence To Expand From Payments Into Full Financial Services. For businesses, RexPOS enables payment acceptance, while RexCredit provides financing options for small and medium-sized enterprises and larger companies. The bank said its services are intended to support customers at different stages of their financial lives, including students, first-time earners, salaried workers, entrepreneurs and growing businesses. Rex Africa Founder, Yinka Odeleye, said the company believes the next phase of banking would be shaped by financial intelligence, with services designed to help customers manage and grow their wealth beyond routine transactions. Chief Technology Officer Opeyemi Emmanuel said the company developed RexCore and Rex Atlas to work together, combining banking infrastructure with AI-powered personalisation. Rex Africa said its operations are supported by Rex Microfinance Bank Limited, which is licensed and regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Eligible deposits are insured by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation, subject to applicable coverage limits. The company also said it operates in line with relevant regulatory and data protection requirements, with safeguards intended to protect customers’ financial information. Since its launch in November 2026, Rex Africa said it has attracted thousands of Nigerians and hundreds of businesses to its platform. Beyond its consumer banking application, the company operates a lending business and a Banking-as-a-Service portal that supports customer accounts, collections and payouts through its proprietary RexCore technology.
